title: Detailed mismatch report — 2026-10-16
historical_note: English translation of the historical record as of 2026-10-16. Counts and implementation status below describe that record, not the current repository. The original Japanese document remains unchanged.
content_lines: # Detailed mismatch report — 2026-10-16
This record distinguishes **2,159 output mismatches in the Python portable model** from differences
observed when executing instructions on ARM / RISC-V. The 2,159 Python findings correspond to 2,157 distinct input IDs
and 30 case IDs. They do not represent 2,159 independent root causes.
The affected operations in the model itself remain unfixed in this historical record.
The reference version of the model is commit `b61b60aced1e808259eb960a291950fea6751abc`.
The counts were collected from a working tree containing additional tests; SHA-256 identifies the actual code and oracles used.
The source summary is `.equilane/test-expansion-20261016-final/summary.json`. A frozen snapshot retaining
publishable relative paths and representative inputs is available at
[`tests/data/mismatch-report-2026-10-16.json`](tests/data/mismatch-report-2026-10-16.json).
The original summary and build artifacts may be absent from other checkouts.
## 1. What was compared
The Python checks first validated each input against its official or explicitly extended contract,
then compared the return value of `load_development_case(...).execute(record)` directly with an independent expected value.
These verdicts did not pass through [`equilane.compare`](src/equilane/compare.py).
The execution paths are [`VerifiedModelMixin.assert_model`](tests/model_test_support.py#L43) and
[`AdversarialModelTests.assert_model`](tests/test_adversarial_models.py#L61).
Expected values came from recorded x86_64 SSE2 probes that never call the Python model.
They were captured by **running x86_64 under Rosetta on arm64 Darwin**, with strict FP, masked exceptions, and FTZ/DAZ disabled.
They are not a comparison between physical Intel and OpenPOWER machines. The frozen FP corpora contain
504 rows in [`rounding-oracles.json`](tests/data/rounding-oracles.json) and
10,708 rows in [`fp-boundary-oracles.json`](tests/data/fp-boundary-oracles.json).
The initial 36 findings use the SSE2 values verified in [`BUG_HUNT.md`](tests/BUG_HUNT.md).
Tests also verify the probes, generation scripts, and digests of the stored corpus rows.
The ordinary development fixture calls the same Python model even when the target is named
Intel / OpenPOWER / ARM / RISC-V. If both sides return the same incorrect value, the fixture comparison passes.
That match proves neither that the model mismatches below were fixed nor that the CPU instructions agree.
See [`fixture._result_record`](src/equilane/fixture.py#L88) for the implementation.

The extended contracts were validated copies of official cases, with additional rounding modes and

Consequently, the 2,053 findings cannot be counted as failures of the official nearest-even contracts.

### 7 groups organized by implementation path
| Group | Mismatch records | Distinct input IDs | Case IDs | Scope |
| Sign of NaNs produced by invalid operations | 28 | 27 | 12 | Official nearest-even |
| NaN payload selection | 78 | 78 | 12 | Official nearest-even |

These 7 categories relate stored output differences to the code at the time of the snapshot.
The family names themselves are not treated as root causes. In particular,
the 84 findings in `fp_boundary_signed_zero_infinity` mix 16 official-contract NaN-sign findings with
68 extended-contract rounding findings, so the categorization takes contract scope into account.
## 3. Representative inputs, expected values, and observations
The `0x...` values below are the bit patterns of individual lanes or scalars.
`×4` means the same value is placed in all 4 lanes. Expected values are the stored SSE2 references;
observations are outputs from the Python model in this arm64 environment.
The JSON `representative_findings` contains 16 examples with complete input records, input IDs,
expected values, observed values, test IDs, and oracle references.
### Official contracts: NaN signs and payloads
| Case / setting | Input | Expected | Observed model output |
Example 1 is `+inf + -inf`; the expected and observed values differ in the NaN sign bit.
Example 2 has a quiet NaN as its first argument and a signaling NaN as its second. After quieting,
the expected payload comes from the first argument, whereas the model retains the second argument's payload.
The official cases covering these inputs require `bit_exact` comparison and do not exclude NaNs from their input domains.
Both values being NaNs is insufficient for a match.
The relevant code is [`float_binary_case`](src/equilane/casepack_families.py#L463).
For add / sub / mul, [`_float_from_bits`](src/equilane/casepack_families.py#L179) converts to Python float;
host arithmetic is followed by conversion back through [`_float_to_bits`](src/equilane/casepack_families.py#L184).
This path and its host-dependent NaN propagation correspond to the observed differences.
Division uses a separate bit-arithmetic path and is absent from this official-contract NaN-sign/payload category.
### Validated extended contracts: requested rounding
| Case / setting | Input | Expected | Observed model output |
| `sse2.sqrt.f32x4.default` / toward-positive | a=`0x40000000`×4 | `0x3fb504f4`×4 | `0x3fb504f3`×4 |
Arithmetic example 1 is `1 + 2^-25`, the integer-conversion example is `1.5`, and the integer-to-f32 example is `16,777,217`.
Even when the difference looks tiny, an integer conversion changes the returned integer itself.
The next inputs also show effects on the sign of zero and on rounding to the smallest subnormal.
| Case / setting | Input | Expected | Observed model output |
Requested rounding is present in the inputs, but the following execution paths do not receive it.
These findings cannot all be explained as host-float precision errors.
| Category | Main implementation paths | What the code shows |

| Arithmetic | [`float_binary_case`](src/equilane/casepack_families.py#L463), [`_divide_float_bits`](src/equilane/casepack_families.py#L206), [`_round_ratio_even`](src/equilane/casepack_families.py#L194) | add/sub/mul use host arithmetic. Division rounds an integer ratio to nearest-even. Neither branches on input rounding. |
| Square root | [`sqrt_case`](src/equilane/casepack_families.py#L1162) | Uses `math.sqrt` and bit conversion for positive finite inputs; ignores input rounding. |

| Floating-point to integer | [`conversion_case`](src/equilane/casepack_families.py#L884), [`float_to_scalar_case`](src/equilane/casepack_families.py#L1005), [`_float_to_integer`](src/equilane/casepack_families.py#L830) | `cvt` uses `round()` and `cvtt` uses `math.trunc()`. The requested rounding direction is not passed through. |

| f64 to f32 | [`conversion_case`](src/equilane/casepack_families.py#L884), [`scalar_conversion_case`](src/equilane/casepack_families.py#L919), [`_f64_to_f32`](src/equilane/casepack_families.py#L775) | The conversion uses bit arithmetic, but its helpers are fixed to nearest-even. |

| Integer to floating-point | The same conversion factories and [`_i32_to_f32`](src/equilane/casepack_families.py#L813) | Uses fixed rounding for i32-to-f32, or `float()` followed by bit conversion; ignores input rounding. |
These observations are consistent with requested rounding not being propagated through the implementation.
This snapshot does not constitute a proof of complete IEEE behavior for each row or a result
that can be generalized to every untested input.
### What these computations mean numerically
Bit patterns record distinctions between very close values, NaNs, and signed zeros.
The main reproductions correspond to the following ordinary computations.
| Operation | Actual computation or conversion | Requested result and observed difference |
| f32 addition | `1 + 2^-25` | The f32 spacing near 1 is `2^-23`. Rounding upward should produce the next representable value, `1 + 2^-23`, but the model returns 1. |
| f32 square root | `sqrt(2)` | Stores the irrational value, approximately 1.414…, in f32. The model returns a value 1 step below the upper value required by upward rounding. |
| f32→i32 | Convert `1.5` to an integer | Rounding downward should return 1. The model returns the nearest-even result, 2. |
| f64→f32 | Narrow `1 + 2^-24` to f32 | Exactly halfway between 1 and `1 + 2^-23`. Upward rounding requires the latter, but the model returns 1. |
| i32→f32 | Convert the integer `16,777,217` to f32 | Neighboring f32 values are 16,777,216 and 16,777,218. Upward rounding requires the latter, but the model returns the former. |
The rounding direction determines which side to choose when the true value is not representable.
| Mode | Meaning | `+1.5` to integer | `-1.5` to integer |
| `nearest_even` | Nearest value; choose the even result at a tie | 2 | -2 |
| `toward_negative` | Toward negative infinity | 1 | -2 |
| `toward_positive` | Toward positive infinity | 2 | -1 |
| `toward_zero` | Toward zero | 1 | -1 |
Packed operations calculate every lane. Scalar operations generally calculate only 1 lane, the lowest,
and preserve the others. For example, `_mm_add_ss(a, b)` adds the lowest f32 values and copies the upper 3 lanes
from `a`. `_mm_cvtsd_ss(a, b)` converts the lowest f64 in `b` to f32 and
preserves the upper 3 lanes of `a`. For `_mm_sqrt_sd(a, b)`, the computed lowest lane likewise comes from `b`
and the preserved upper lane comes from `a`. This framework's unary wrapper calls `_mm_sqrt_sd(a, a)`,
so both the square root and the preserved lane come from 1 input.
Conversely, conversions that return an integer scalar, such as `_mm_cvtss_si32`, use the lowest input lane
without copying any upper lanes to their results.
A NaN represents “not a number”; its payload is an identifying bit pattern in its significand.
The quiet/signaling distinction is also encoded in bits. A NaN sign bit does not imply ordinary positive/negative ordering,
but both the sign and payload are compared by `bit_exact`.
The NaN categories in this report concern which input supplies those bits and which sign an invalid operation generates.
Output-mismatch counts alone do not establish mismatches in FP exception flags.
`+0` and `-0` compare equal numerically but have different bit patterns.
They are recorded separately to test the sign of rounded zero and the choice of input
returned by min/max on equal values.
### Examples of operations checked on the matching side
The checks cover more than FP mismatches. The following examples explain integer, lane, memory,
and bitcast computations. These 7 inputs were also contract-validated, passed to the model, and checked against expected values.
**They are excluded from the 2,159 mismatch records.** Their complete details, including expectations, are stored in
JSON `matching_operation_examples`. They do not mean that every input to all 254 operations matches.
Array entries run from **lane 0 (least significant), lane 1, …**, left to right.
Memory bytes are listed in ascending address order; multibyte integers are read as little endian.
| Operation / Guide | Input and computation | Result checked | Corresponding existing tests |

| 8-bit integer wrapping and saturation / [`_mm_add_epi8`](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html#text=_mm_add_epi8), [`_mm_adds_epi8`](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html#text=_mm_adds_epi8) | `127 + 1` in each i8 lane | Wrapping retains 8 bits, yielding `0x80` (-128 as signed); signed saturation stops at 127. These additions have different semantics. | [Wrapping](tests/test_integer_boundary_models.py#L135), [signed / unsigned saturation](tests/test_integer_boundary_models.py#L151) |

| Lane shuffle / [`_mm_shuffle_epi32`](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html#text=_mm_shuffle_epi32) | 4 lanes `[a0,a1,a2,a3]` with `imm8=27` (`0x1b`) | The 2-bit selectors, from low to high, are `3,2,1,0`, returning `[a3,a2,a1,a0]`. | [All imm8 values and preserved lanes](tests/test_integer_boundary_models.py#L393) |

| Large shift count / [`_mm_sll_epi32`](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html#text=_mm_sll_epi32) | Shift i32 lanes `[1,2,-1,-2147483648]` left by the count's low 64 bits, `2^32+1` | All lanes become 0. Do not truncate the count to a low-32-bit value of 1 or reduce it modulo the lane width. | [Low 64 bits of count](tests/test_integer_boundary_models.py#L342), [ignored upper count lane](tests/test_integer_boundary_models.py#L361) |

| Unaligned load / [`_mm_loadu_si128`](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html#text=_mm_loadu_si128) | Read 16 bytes `00 01 … 0f` starting at buffer offset 3 | i32 bits are `[0x03020100,0x07060504,0x0b0a0908,0x0f0e0d0c]`. The buffer stays unchanged; lane and byte order are preserved. | [Offsets, guards, and separate allocations](tests/test_integer_boundary_models.py#L495) |

| Unaligned store / [`_mm_storeu_si128`](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html#text=_mm_storeu_si128) | Write 16 bytes `80 81 … 8f` at buffer offset 3 | Only byte positions 3–18 are replaced. Guards on both sides and a separate `unrelated` buffer stay unchanged. | [All-buffer load/store comparison](tests/test_integer_boundary_models.py#L495) |

| Bitcast / [`_mm_castps_si128`](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html#text=_mm_castps_si128) | Reinterpret f32 `[0x80000000,0,0,0]`, including `-0`, as i32 | Every bit stays unchanged. The first i32 is -2147483648 when interpreted as signed; this differs from numerical conversion to 0. | [All 128 bits, 1 bit at a time](tests/test_adversarial_models.py#L263) |
These expectations use fixed-width integer arithmetic, explicit clamping, and independent byte operations.
When testing all imm8 values for shuffle/shift, values beyond the official allowlist are distinguished
as explicit validation extensions. The shuffle example `27` above is itself in the official allowlist.

### Mapping to the Intel Intrinsics Guide

The source is the [Intel Intrinsics Guide](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html). Its [official offline distribution](https://cdrdv2.intel.com/v1/dl/getContent/671338) was retrieved on 2026-10-16; the verified version was `3.6.9`, with data date attribute `07/12/2024`.

The next 30 rows match each official case's Intel binding to the same-named Guide intrinsic. Complete prototypes, actual wrapper calls, and Guide search links are also stored in JSON `intrinsic_mappings`.

**The `sse2` case-ID namespace is distinct from an individual intrinsic's ISA.** Each case has minimum Intel profile `sse2`, but the Guide identifies 12 rows, including `_mm_add_ps`, as SSE and the other 18 as SSE2. Do not interpret this prefix as the ISA in which each instruction first appeared.

| `sse2.sub.f64x2.scalar` | 33 | [`_mm_sub_sd`](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html#text=_mm_sub_sd) | SSE2 | `SUBSD` / `<emmintrin.h>` | Perform subtraction on the lowest f64 lane, preserving the upper 1 lane of a. |
**Some bindings restrict the arguments.** The Guide's `_mm_sqrt_sd(a, b)` takes 2 arguments,
but the [unary wrapper](10_official_suite/intel/f64x2.c#L12) calls `_mm_sqrt_sd(a, a)`.
Both the lowest-lane square root and the preserved upper lane come from input `a`. The Guide prototype and framework case signature therefore do not necessarily match directly.
Additional ARM native diagnostics cover these 2 operations, which are not among the 30 Python-mismatch cases above.
| Case corresponding to ARM diagnostic | Guide intrinsic | ISA | Instruction / header | Computation |

| `sse2.min.f64x2.default` | [`_mm_min_pd`](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html#text=_mm_min_pd) | SSE2 | `MINPD` / `<emmintrin.h>` | Select the minimum of each of 2 f64 lanes. |

The Guide establishes mappings among operations, types, and instructions. It is not claimed to be
the sole source for every expected NaN sign/payload bit in this report. Concrete expected bits come from
separate observational evidence captured by strict SSE2/Rosetta execution. Read the Guide mapping and execution provenance separately.
JSON `case_counts` gives each case's breakdown by rounding mode and contract scope; `family_counts` gives the family breakdown.
The absence of a mismatch does not certify a case as correct for every input.
No mismatches were observed in this record's new comparison, min/max, bitwise, and memory matrices,
but those results apply only to the specified input sets.
## 5. 6 observations from ARM native wrappers
These results execute the ARM C wrappers on this arm64 Mac without calling the Python model.
[`test_arm_wrappers.c`](tests/native/test_arm_wrappers.c#L145) asserts 4,596 control checks and
prints the following 6 examples beside their SSE2/Rosetta references. These 6 examples are diagnostic output, not failed assertions,
so both the executable and CTest exit with code 0 even when the differences are printed.
| Input / operation (lane 0 for f64 results) | SSE2/Rosetta reference | ARM observation |
These hexadecimal values are IEEE lane encodings or i32 integer encodings.
The paths using ARM [`vaddq_f64` / `vminq_f64` / `vmaxq_f64`](10_official_suite/arm/f64x2.c#L6) and
the [`FCVTNS` conversion helpers](10_official_suite/arm/neon_helpers.h)
do not adjust these differences to reproduce SSE2 values.
They are recorded as observed instruction-semantic differences, not added to the Python-model defect count.
Nor do these 6 examples represent an exhaustive comparison of all 254 cases.
## 6. RISC-V / RVV comparison under QEMU
[`test_riscv_suite.py`](tests/native/test_riscv_suite.py) supplies 3 inputs to each of 254 raw C wrappers
and compares x86_64 SSE2/Rosetta execution against RV64/RVV 1.0 execution under QEMU.
The same RVV ELF is executed with VLEN 128 / 256.
The source summary reports Clang 22.1.8, Apple Clang 21.0.0, and QEMU 11.1.0.
| VLEN | Inputs compared | Matches | Mismatches |
Both VLEN settings produce identical mismatching sample names and results. There are **12 distinct mismatching samples**,
not 24 distinct differences.
The 12 samples are the NaN-containing input `#2` for add / sub / mul × f32 / f64 × packed / scalar.
All 12 examples, including exact sample names, complete operands, expected values, and observations,
are stored in JSON `native_observations.riscv.differences`.
For example, `add_f32x4#2` has the following inputs:
```text
SSE2 reference lanes = [0x7fc00042, 0x7fc00035, 0xffc00000, 0x7fc00042]
RVV observed lanes  = [0x7fc00000, 0x7fc00000, 0x7fc00000, 0x7fc00000]
The original summary records the same results as SSE2=`4200c07f3500c07f0000c0ff4200c07f` and
These are **byte sequences in memory order**. Each group of 4 little-endian bytes represents one f32 lane;
the entire string must not be interpreted as one hexadecimal number or ULP distance.
The arithmetic paths use RVV intrinsics in [`riscv/f32x4.c`](10_official_suite/riscv/f32x4.c#L319),
[`riscv/f64x2.c`](10_official_suite/riscv/f64x2.c#L6), and
[`rvv128.h`](10_official_suite/riscv/rvv128.h#L111).
The observed NaNs are canonical NaNs, unlike the SSE2 reference payloads and signs.
These observations cannot be generalized to other inputs, all rounding modes, or all FP exceptions.
They execute RISC-V machine code under QEMU; they do not verify physical RISC-V hardware or the Linux native runner.
The comparison tool retains the mismatches and returns exit code 1.
## 7. Scope of OpenPOWER and the encoded ABI
For OpenPOWER / ppc64le, this historical record verified the cross-build of 6 objects targeting POWER8 + AltiVec + VSX.
It did not measure output on physical OpenPOWER hardware. The OpenPOWER JSON field `differences: []`
means “not measured,” not “0 mismatches” or “everything matches.”
The 254 raw wrappers for each of 4 targets and the canonical encoded ABI have different execution coverage.
At the time of this record, only the 3 add / set1 / shuffle examples were connected to the shared ABI.
The RISC-V encoded adapter had been cross-compiled, but linking and execution with Linux libc / fenv were unverified.
Cross-builds and raw-wrapper execution alone do not establish a complete set of specification-compliant
native result manifests. See [Native status](documentation/native-status.json) for details.
## 8. Reproduction steps
Run the following from the repository root for small reproductions of the model mismatches.
In the arm64 environment and model version used for this record, they print mismatches and exit with code 1.
Host-dependent Python behavior means other CPUs or Python versions may produce different counts.
```sh
PYTHONPATH=src:tests .venv/bin/python -m unittest \
test_adversarial_models.AdversarialModelTests.test_add_opposite_infinities_returns_negative_indefinite_nan
PYTHONPATH=src:tests .venv/bin/python -m unittest \
test_adversarial_models.AdversarialModelTests.test_requested_rounding_in_arithmetic
.venv/bin/python -m unittest discover -s tests -p test_fp_boundary_models.py
To record the complete run in a new output location:
```sh
mkdir -p build
report_run=$(mktemp -d build/mismatch-run.XXXXXX)
PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python -m equilane.quality_runner \
--project-root . --output "$report_run/quality" \
> "$report_run/summary.stdout.json"
`quality_runner` rejects an existing output directory, so each run creates a new parent directory
and writes into a nonexistent `quality` child. Standard output is stored outside that child.
This command does not overwrite the frozen snapshot. An ordinary quality run uses stored expectations
instead of rerunning the SSE2 probes. [`BUG_HUNT.md`](tests/BUG_HUNT.md) describes the strict-FP probe builds
and `--verify` steps for independently recapturing and validating NaN and rounding expectations.
Example: extract a complete representative input from the frozen record:
```sh
.venv/bin/python - <<'PY'
import json
from pathlib import Path
snapshot = json.loads(Path('tests/data/mismatch-report-2026-10-16.json').read_text())
finding = next(row for row in snapshot['representative_findings']
if row['report_example_id'] == 'rounding_arithmetic')
print(json.dumps(finding, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2))
PY
Rerun ARM raw wrappers, recapture and compare RVV results, and cross-build all targets:
```sh
cmake -S . -B build/native -DBUILD_TESTING=ON -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
cmake --build build/native --parallel
./build/native/ioitf_arm_wrappers_selftest
.venv/bin/python tests/native/test_riscv_suite.py
./10_official_suite/cross-compile.sh
ARM execution requires an arm64 environment; RVV capture requires LLVM Clang and QEMU; the SSE2 reference requires an x86_64 execution environment.
Use Rosetta to execute the reference on Apple Silicon.
The RVV comparison produces a summary recording mismatches even when it exits with code 1.
